title: Memory Safety and Common Memory Errors
learningObjectives: Define the central safety or tracing concept.
Identify a common failure pattern or diagnostic step.
Trace a small example and explain the result.
Describe a safer or more systematic approach.
Apply the idea to a simple scenario.

understand.concept: Memory safety means program operations do not access memory in invalid or unintended ways. Common problems in languages with manual or low-level memory access include out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, dangling pointers, double release, and unintended aliasing. Managed languages reduce some categories of risk but still can have logical bugs, unsafe interfaces, or resource leaks.
understand.whyItMatters: Memory safety failures can cause crashes, corruption, security vulnerabilities, or unpredictable behavior. Understanding the common categories helps programmers use safer APIs, validate boundaries, and avoid risky memory operations.
understand.analogy: A fence around a garden helps keep movement within a safe area; software checks must be specific and correct, not just decorative.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is simplified; actual program behavior depends on language, runtime, and system rules.

explain.narrative: Review the relevant data, operations, and boundary conditions. For safety topics, check whether inputs and lifetimes are valid and use safe APIs. For debugging, trace values through the program, compare expected and actual results, and identify the earliest incorrect step. Confirm a fix with tests rather than relying on one observed output.

commonMistakes: Assuming input values or indexes are always valid.
Relying on one test case only.
Fixing the final symptom without finding the first incorrect step.
Changing multiple variables in a debugging experiment.
